description: We are recent Computer Science and Software Engineering graduates passionate about AI, software engineering, and space technology. We’re interested in the Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map challenge and looking for teammates skilled in VR, game design, 3D/interactive experiences, or knowledgeable in Mars and planetary science. We’re open to ideas and excited to build something meaningful together.
summary:
MARSWALK is a web-based Mars exploration simulator that helps crews plan and carry out multiple scientific tasks within one journey. It addresses NASA’s “Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map” challenge by combining Mars mapping data with mission planning, resource estimates, and communication tools.

Communication delays between Mars and Earth make immediate guidance impractical. MARSWALK allows the Earth team to prepare routes and tasks that astronauts can access during exploration without waiting for instructions at every step. The crew can explore in a first-person 3D view, record findings, and send updates, while the Earth team monitors received progress.

Using terrain data, previous mission information, recorded environmental conditions, and estimated time and oxygen budgets, MARSWALK helps users assess what fits into a mission. Its adaptive planning feature compares the original plan with revised task selections when circumstances change.

More than a map, MARSWALK demonstrates how crews could make informed decisions, prioritise scientific work, and manage limited resources while exploring the Martian surface.
details:
1. What does the project do and how does it work?

MARSWALK is a web-based Mars exploration simulator developed for the “Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map” challenge. It combines Mars mapping data, mission planning, scientific observations, and crew monitoring to help users organise multiple activities within one surface journey.

The system has two connected workspaces:

  • Earth team: Selects routes, assigns astronauts and scientific tasks, sets mission budgets, and monitors received progress and findings.
  • Mars crew: Reviews the assigned mission, completes preparation checks, and begins a first-person 3D walk.

During exploration, users can record notes, upload photographs, record audio, complete tasks, and communicate with the Earth team. The interface displays remaining mission time, estimated oxygen endurance, terrain information, and available environmental data.

When an investigation takes longer than planned, users can compare their original plan with an adjusted task selection that accounts for the remaining resources and return journey. Completed missions are saved in a mission log.

2. What benefits does the project have?

  • Connected planning: Combines routes, scientific tasks, crew information, and resource estimates in one mission.
  • Support during communication delays: Keeps the assigned plan and task information accessible to the Mars crew while awaiting Earth-team responses.
  • Resource awareness: Shows how walking, investigations, and return travel affect mission time and estimated oxygen endurance.
  • Adaptive task selection: Helps users prioritise scientific activities when the original plan no longer fits.
  • Organised findings: Stores observations, messages, task progress, and completed mission records for review.
  • Shared monitoring: Allows the Earth team to follow received crew progress, with timestamps showing how old the information is.

3. What is the intended impact?

MARSWALK helps users understand the decisions involved in exploring Mars: where to travel, what to investigate, how long to spend, and when to return.

Our approach was informed by NASA’s BASALT analogue research, which studied scientific fieldwork with remote support under simulated Mars communication constraints, including five- and fifteen-minute one-way delays.

MARSWALK applies these ideas through accessible mission plans, delayed messaging, and resource-aware task selection. The crew can continue working from an agreed plan while the Earth team reviews incoming findings and provides further guidance.

The intended impact is an educational and mission-rehearsal tool that makes the relationship between terrain, scientific objectives, communication delays, and limited resources easier to understand. It is a prototype, not a certified navigation or life-support system.

4. What tools, programming languages, and data were used?

Development tools

  • React and TypeScript: User interfaces, mission interactions, and planning calculations.
  • Three.js: Interactive Mars globe, first-person terrain visualisation, and 3D model rendering.
  • Leaflet: Interactive 2D maps.
  • Vite: Development environment and production builds.
  • Node.js: Backend services and shared mission updates.
  • Supabase PostgreSQL: Hosted storage for mission state, messages, observations, and history.
  • SQLite: Local database during development.
  • Vercel: Website and API deployment.
  • Git and GitHub: Version control and collaboration.
  • Rubik and Lucide: Interface typography and icons.

Scientific data and visual resources

  • NASA/USGS Viking imagery: Photographic texture for the Mars globe.
  • HiRISE imagery and elevation models: Regional terrain visualisation and elevation-based calculations.
  • Perseverance traverse and waypoint records: Named locations and recorded rover paths in Jezero Crater.
  • Perseverance MEDA records: Historical temperature and available atmospheric pressure information.
  • NASA science descriptions: Geological and previous exploration context for supported locations.
  • NASA life-support reference values: Baseline assumptions for oxygen-demand estimates.
  • PhysioNet BIDMC dataset: Optional replay of recorded heart rate, breathing rate, and blood oxygen measurements. This is hospital patient data, not astronaut data.
  • DigitalSpace Corporation astronaut model, distributed through NASA 3D Resources: An illustrative model for suit monitoring.

The BIDMC recording is bundled with the project and read from a converted JSON file when reference replay is enabled. It is separate from the automatically generated demonstration health readings.

No physical spacesuit, health sensor, or astronaut positioning hardware is connected. Crew movement is simulated, and environmental measurements are historical records rather than live Martian weather forecasts.

5. What equations and algorithms does the project use?

MARSWALK uses explicit calculations to estimate travel time, oxygen demand, and the tasks that can fit into a mission. Walking speed, task durations, priorities, and reserves are editable scenario inputs.

A. Travel time

Travel time (minutes) = Distance (metres) ÷ Walking speed (metres/second) ÷ 60

Example:

660 ÷ 1.1 ÷ 60 = 10 minutes

Route distance comes from mapped coordinates. Walking speed is an assumed or simulated pace, so the result is an estimate rather than a proven astronaut completion time.

B. Total mission time

Required time = Outward travel + Task time + Return travel + Time reserve

Example:

10 minutes outward + 15 minutes observing + 10 minutes returning + 10 minutes reserve = 45 minutes

This checks whether the planned journey and scientific activities fit within the mission duration.

C. Oxygen demand

Oxygen demand (grams) = Consumption rate (grams/hour) × Duration (minutes) ÷ 60

The model uses a baseline metabolic oxygen consumption rate of 86 grams per person per hour, drawn from NASA’s Life Support Baseline Values and Assumptions Document, with configurable additional losses.

For a 60-minute mission with a 15-minute oxygen reserve:

86 × (60 + 15) ÷ 60 = 107.5 grams

This is a planning estimate. Tank endurance is entered by the user; the system does not measure tank contents or calculate a certified tank-filling requirement.

D. Available time for scientific tasks

Time available = Remaining mission time − Time reserve

Oxygen time available = Remaining oxygen endurance − Oxygen reserve

Task capacity = The smaller of these two values − Remaining travel time

If the result is negative, task capacity is set to zero. Remaining travel includes the return journey.

The complete expression is:

Task capacity = max(0, min(B − Rt, E − Ro) − travel_minutes)

B is remaining mission time, E is remaining oxygen endurance, and Rt and Ro are their respective reserves. All values are in minutes.

For multiple astronauts, the system considers the crew member with the least oxygen endurance available above their personal reserve.

E. Adaptive task selection

Goal: Select the combination of tasks with the highest total priority.

Constraint: Total selected task duration must not exceed task capacity.

The system uses a 0/1 knapsack algorithm, meaning each task is either included or excluded. Priorities are assigned by the mission team.

This helps identify which activities can still fit when additional investigation time or a change in walking pace affects the plan. Tasks remain on the selected route; the algorithm does not optimise an unrestricted journey across every destination on Mars.

F. Terrain-aware route alternatives

Segment cost = Horizontal segment length × [1 + 4 × (Absolute elevation change ÷ Horizontal segment length)]

For supported elevation coverage, Dijkstra’s algorithm searches for a route with the lowest combined cost across the terrain grid.

This penalises elevation changes and excludes missing terrain cells or slopes above the selected scenario limit. The multiplier 4 is a project setting, not a validated astronaut safety threshold.

G. Communication timing

Delivery time (seconds) = Sent time (seconds) + Rounded one-way delay (minutes × 60)

Example:

120 + (5 × 60) = 420 seconds

A message sent at mission time 120 seconds with a five-minute delay becomes available at 420 seconds. A reply requires the return communication delay and the Earth team’s review time.

H. Remaining resources

Remaining mission time = Initial mission duration − Elapsed mission minutes

Remaining oxygen endurance = Initial oxygen endurance − Elapsed mission minutes

Oxygen endurance is bounded at zero. Investigation stops continue consuming mission time and modelled oxygen endurance.

These calculations are implemented in files including preflight.ts, adaptivePlanning.ts, terrainAlternatives.ts, planComparison.ts, crewOperations.ts, and commManager.ts.

6. How is the project creative and innovative?

MARSWALK connects a visual Mars map with the decisions users make during an expedition.

Its main distinguishing feature is the comparison between an original mission plan and an adjusted task selection. When the crew changes pace or spends longer investigating a location, the system shows which tasks can still fit within the remaining time and oxygen budgets.

The project also connects first-person exploration with an Earth-team monitoring workspace. Observations, task updates, health demonstrations, and messages belong to the same shared mission, while communication timing affects when reports become visible.

The recommendations use explainable calculations and optimisation algorithms. Users can understand why a task fits, why it is excluded, and how a change affects the return estimate.

7. What factors did the team consider during development?

  • Usability: Minimal text, readable controls, consistent typography, and accessible information during exploration.
  • Communication limitations: The crew can consult its assigned plan while waiting for responses, and the Earth team can see the age of received reports.
  • Mission resources: Travel and observations must account for return time and reserves.
  • Data coverage: Missing terrain or environmental information remains visibly unavailable rather than being presented as a measured value.
  • Scientific transparency: Recorded data, editable assumptions, and generated demonstration values are distinguished.
  • Crew monitoring: Blood oxygen, tank endurance, and suit measurements are treated as separate quantities.
  • Shared mission state: Both teams use the same stored mission, with one active expedition at a time.
  • Validation: Automated tests check calculation behaviour, task selection, mission transitions, and shared data handling. These tests verify software behaviour, not real astronaut performance.
  • Resource attribution: External datasets, models, fonts, and software are documented with their sources and applicable licence notices.
